warmup.q: A Temporal activity charges a card. The worker is killed with kill -9 after the issuer approved the charge but before the worker reported success. What happens next?
options: The charge is lost and the workflow fails
Temporal knows the charge happened and moves on to the next step
After the activity's timeout, Temporal runs the charge again, so the card is charged twice unless the call carries an idempotency key
The workflow starts over from the beginning and repeats every step
warmup.why: The server only learns an activity's result when a worker reports it. Here it saw an attempt start and never finish, so after the start-to-close timeout it retries the activity. Activities are at-least-once; the engine records progress once, but the side effect can happen twice. The fourth option is half right: a new worker does re-run the workflow code from the top, but steps already recorded in the history return their saved results instead of running again.

sections.h: Three calls, and the process can die between any two
sections.html:
An order in your shop takes three calls to three systems: charge the card at the issuer, reserve the item in the warehouse, hand the parcel to the courier. As plain code it is three lines:

val chargeId = bank.charge(order)
val reservation = warehouse.reserve(order)
courier.ship(order, reservation)

Now a deploy restarts the pod between the first and the second line. The card is charged and nothing is reserved, and nothing will ever run the second line for this order: the only record that the order was in progress was the stack of a thread that no longer exists. You can't wrap the three calls in one database transaction either. They go to three systems, and one of them is a card network that takes no part in your transactions. (The Transactions track's lesson on atomic commit shows what committing across machines takes, and why few systems offer it.)

The first fix that comes to mind is to run the whole order again after a crash. That turns every crash after the charge into a second charge. The classic fix is to write progress down. Add a status column to orders and update it after each step, in its own local transaction: NEW, CHARGED, RESERVED, SHIPPED. A sweeper job runs every minute, finds orders stuck halfway (not SHIPPED and untouched for five minutes) and continues each one from its recorded status.

The Try runs 10,000 orders through these strategies, with a crash at each of six points (before and after each side effect) with probability 0.5%. With no recovery, 247 orders end charged and never shipped. Restarting from the top ships them all and charges 247 cards twice. The status column cuts that to 50, and those 50 are the crashes that landed after the bank charged but before the UPDATE committed. That gap never closes, because no local transaction can include the bank's side effect. Only an idempotency key on the charge (order-42/charge, as in lesson 4 of this track) brings it to zero.

So a status column works, with keys, and many payment systems run this way today. The cost shows as the processes multiply. Each one rebuilds the same machinery: a lock so two sweepers don't take the same order, retries with backoff, a timeout per step, the keys. A rule like "refund if the courier hasn't collected within three days" becomes another status and another polling query. The process itself is spread over a column, a cron job and a handler per status, and adding a step means migrating every order already in flight to a new set of statuses. Brandur Leach's 2017 design for Stripe-style idempotency keys in Postgres is this approach done carefully: local work committed in atomic phases between external calls, with a recovery point recorded after each one.

try.title: Crash 10,000 orders four ways
steps: Open CrashBetweenStepsDemo.kt. It is plain Kotlin, no Temporal: each order runs the three steps, and a seeded random kills the process at one of six points.
Predict which strategies leave double charges, and how the status column compares with restarting from the top.
Run it from the labs folder with the command below.
Change CRASH_CHANCE to 0.02, run it again, and see which numbers grow.

code.title: CrashBetweenStepsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.enc.l05.demo import kotlin.random.Random /** * 10,000 orders run charge -> reserve -> ship, and the process sometimes dies. Each step has two places to die: * before its side effect, and after the side effect but before the program has written down that it happened. * Four ways to recover, and what each leaves behind. Plain Kotlin, no Temporal. */ private const val ORDERS = 10_000 private const val CRASH_CHANCE = 0.005 // at each of the 6 points private val STEPS = listOf("charge", "reserve", "ship") private class Outcome { var charges = 0; var reservations = 0; var parcels = 0 var chargedNotShipped = 0; var doubleCharged = 0 } private enum class Recovery { NONE, RESTART_FROM_TOP, STATUS_COLUMN, STATUS_COLUMN_AND_KEYS } private fun run(recovery: Recovery, seed: Int): Outcome { val rnd = Random(seed) val out = Outcome() repeat(ORDERS) { n -> var status = 0 // the status column: how many steps are recorded as done val keysSeen = HashSet<String>() // the bank's idempotency keys, for the last strategy var chargesForOrder = 0 var finished = false var attempts = 0 while (!finished && attempts < 10) { attempts++ var crashed = false val from = if (recovery == Recovery.STATUS_COLUMN || recovery == Recovery.STATUS_COLUMN_AND_KEYS) status else 0 for (i in from until STEPS.size) { if (rnd.nextDouble() < CRASH_CHANCE) { crashed = true; break } // died before the side effect when (STEPS[i]) { // the side effect "charge" -> { val key = "order-$n/charge" if (recovery != Recovery.STATUS_COLUMN_AND_KEYS || keysSeen.add(key)) { out.charges++; chargesForOrder++ } } "reserve" -> out.reservations++ "ship" -> out.parcels++ } if (rnd.nextDouble() < CRASH_CHANCE) { crashed = true; break } // died after it, before recording it status = i + 1 // UPDATE orders SET status = ... (one local transaction) } if (!crashed) finished = true if (recovery == Recovery.NONE) break // nobody comes back for it } if (chargesForOrder > 0 && !finished) out.chargedNotShipped++ if (chargesForOrder > 1) out.doubleCharged++ } return out } fun main() { println("$ORDERS orders; at each of 6 points the process dies with probability $CRASH_CHANCE") println("%-26s %8s %18s %14s".format("recovery", "charges", "charged, unshipped", "double charges")) for (r in Recovery.entries) { val o = run(r, seed = 7) println("%-26s %8d %18d %14d".format(r.name.lowercase().replace('_', ' '), o.charges, o.chargedNotShipped, o.doubleCharged)) } }

try.expect:
10000 orders; at each of 6 points the process dies with probability 0.005
recovery                    charges charged, unshipped double charges
none                           9959                247              0
restart from top              10255                  0            247
status column                 10051                  0             50
status column and keys        10000                  0              0

With 0.02 the rows read 901 charged and unshipped, 936 double charges for restarting from the top, 200 for the status column and still 0 with keys. The status column's 50 (or 200) are the crashes between the bank's charge and the UPDATE that records it: about a fifth of the crashes that come after a charge, because one of the five crash points after the charge lies in that gap. The key closes it, because the bank, not your database, remembers what it already did.

sections.h: When a step fails for good: sagas and compensation
sections.html:
A crash is a step that didn't finish. A refusal is different: the warehouse answers that the item is out of stock, and asking again won't change that. By then the card is charged. You can't roll a card charge back the way a database rolls back a transaction, because the money has moved and the customer may already see it in their banking app. What you can do is take a new action that cancels its effect: a refund.

Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem named this pattern in 1987. A saga is a long-running process split into steps T1, T2 and so on, each a transaction of its own, and each paired with a compensating step (C1, C2 and so on) that semantically undoes it. If a step fails for good, the saga runs the compensations of the steps already done, newest first. For the order, the charge is undone by a refund and the reservation by a release. If the reservation fails, refund. If the courier refuses the parcel, release the item, then refund.

Three properties of sagas catch people out. A compensation is a second action, and the first stays on the record: the customer's statement shows a charge and a refund, the card network may keep a fee, and a confirmation email that went out stays sent. A saga has no isolation: between the charge and the refund, anyone can see the order in its charged-but-not-reserved state, including the customer, the fraud service and tonight's reports. And a compensation must not fail for good. A refund that can't go through becomes a support ticket, so compensations are retried until they succeed, and they need idempotency keys as much as the forward steps do.

Order the steps so that whatever is hardest to undo comes last. Releasing a reservation is cheap and invisible; a refund is visible; a parcel in a courier's van can't be undone by any API call. So ship goes last, and nothing after it may fail.

Where does a saga keep track of which steps are done and which compensations are due? In the hand-built version, in the status column again, with extra statuses for each compensation. The next section moves that bookkeeping into an engine.

sections.h: Durable execution: record every step, then replay the code
sections.html:
Durable execution keeps the three-line program and makes it survive the crash. It splits the program in two. Activities do the work that touches the outside world: charge, reserve, ship. They run in ordinary threads, may fail and may be retried. The workflow is the code that decides what happens next, with its ifs, loops, waits and compensations, and it never touches the outside world itself.

Here is how Temporal runs it. A Temporal server (a cluster with its own database; version 1.32 in November 2026) keeps an append-only event history for every workflow run. Workers are your processes, and they poll the server for tasks. When a worker runs the workflow code and reaches activities.charge(...), the SDK does not call the bank. It sends the server a command, schedule activity Charge. The server appends ActivityTaskScheduled to the history and hands the task to an activity worker, which calls the bank and reports back. The server appends ActivityTaskCompleted with the charge id, and the workflow code carries on with that value. Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofHours(24)) becomes a timer: the server records TimerStarted, and no thread waits for a day.

Now kill the worker while the order sleeps. The history is safe in the server. A day later the timer fires and another worker gets the task. It has never seen this order, so it replays: it runs the workflow function from the first line, against the history. When the code reaches charge, the SDK finds the completed event and returns the recorded charge id at once, without calling the bank. The same happens for reserve, and the sleep returns because its timer has already fired. Then the code reaches ship, which has no event yet, so this time the SDK schedules it for real.

This is the write-ahead log from the Storage engines track, applied to a program. Write each step's result durably, and after a crash, rebuild the state by reading the log from the start.

Two practical details. A healthy worker rarely replays: it keeps recent workflows in memory, and the server sends a workflow's next task to that same worker (sticky execution). If the worker dies, the server gives the task to any worker after a short timeout, 5 seconds by default in the Java SDK. And Temporal has no released Kotlin SDK. From Kotlin you use the Java SDK, 1.40, with the temporal-kotlin module, which adds builders such as ActivityOptions { ... }.

refs.title: Temporal: Event History walkthrough with the Java SDK

video.title: Durable execution: record every step, then replay

sections.h: Exactly once means recorded once, so side effects still need keys
sections.html:
Look again at the moment between the bank's answer and the ActivityTaskCompleted event. Suppose the activity worker charged the card and died before it could report back. The server knows only that an attempt started and never finished. After the activity's start-to-close timeout (the longest one attempt may take) it schedules another attempt, and the card is charged again. No engine can close this gap, for the same reason the status column couldn't: the bank's side effect and the engine's record of it are two writes in two systems.

So activities run at least once. Temporal's default activity retry policy never gives up: it waits 1 second, then doubles the wait up to 100 seconds between attempts. (Workflows themselves don't retry by default.) Temporal's own docs ask you to make activities idempotent, and the engine makes it easy. The workflow ID is stable for the life of the run, and each activity's input is recorded once in the history, so a key built from them, "$workflowId/charge", is the same on every retry and every replay. Pass it to the bank, and the bank turns the second attempt into a replay. In the Try, the charge activity runs twice either way; the card is charged twice without the key and once with it.

That is what "exactly once" means in these engines: the workflow's progress, its decisions and recorded results, is applied once. Here is how the main ones compare in November 2026:

Engine Where progress is recorded How it resumes
Temporal (server 1.32, Java SDK 1.40) an event history in the Temporal cluster, which workers poll replays the workflow code against the history
Restate (1.8, Java and Kotlin SDK 2.11) a journal per invocation, in a Restate server that sits in front of your services and calls them replays the handler, skipping completed steps
DBOS Transact (Java 1.2) checkpoint rows in your own PostgreSQL; a library, no extra server re-runs the workflow, returning saved step outputs
AWS Step Functions, Standard the execution history of a state machine written in JSON moves to the next state; no code replay
AWS Lambda durable functions (since December 2025) checkpoints written by the durable execution SDK re-runs the handler from the start, skipping checkpointed steps

Each one qualifies the claim. Restate says an invocation runs exactly once regardless of failures, yet by the argument above a side effect inside a step can still repeat if the crash comes before the step's result is journaled. DBOS says steps are tried at least once and never re-executed once they complete. Step Functions Standard is exactly-once unless you configure Retry, and its Express type is at-least-once (asynchronous) or at-most-once (synchronous). Read every exactly-once claim as effectively once: at-least-once execution plus deduplication by key. The Messaging track meets the same claim in Kafka's transactions.

try.title: A charge that runs twice
steps: Open AtLeastOnceDemo.kt. StepsImpl in DemoOrders.kt charges the bank and then, on attempt 1 only, throws as if the worker had died before reporting back.
Predict, for a bank that ignores keys and one that honours them, how often the charge activity runs and how often the card is charged.

code.title: AtLeastOnceDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.enc.l05.demo /** * The first charge attempt moves the money and then dies before reporting back. Temporal retries it. * Run twice: against a bank that ignores idempotency keys, and against one that honours them. */ fun main() { quiet() for (honorKeys in listOf(false, true)) { newEnv().use { env -> val bank = FakeBank(honorKeys) val worker = startWorker(env.workflowClient, "worker-1", OrderV1::class.java, StepsImpl(bank, crashAfterCharge = true)) val result = startOrder(env.workflowClient, "order-7").getResult(String::class.java) println("bank honours keys=$honorKeys: $result, charge activity ran ${worker.steps.runs("charge")}x, card charged ${bank.charges.get()}x") if (!honorKeys) { env.workflowClient.fetchHistory("order-7").events .filter { it.hasActivityTaskScheduledEventAttributes() || it.hasActivityTaskStartedEventAttributes() || it.hasActivityTaskCompletedEventAttributes() } .take(3) .forEach { println(" " + describe(it)) } } worker.kill() } } }

try.expect:
bank honours keys=false: SHIPPED, charge activity ran 2x, card charged 2x
      5  ACTIVITY_TASK_SCHEDULED      Charge
      6  ACTIVITY_TASK_STARTED        attempt 2 on worker-1
      7  ACTIVITY_TASK_COMPLETED
bank honours keys=true: SHIPPED, charge activity ran 2x, card charged 1x

The workflow sees one charge either way: one scheduled event, one completed event. The failed first attempt left no event of its own; the server retried inside the activity and wrote down only the attempt that finished, attempt 2. The bank, though, saw two requests. Only the key order-7/charge, the same on both attempts, let it answer the second with the first charge.

sections.h: Changing workflow code under runs in flight
sections.html:
Replay has one condition: given the same history, the workflow code must make the same decisions in the same order. So workflow code may not use anything that can differ between runs: Random, UUID.randomUUID(), the system clock, Thread.sleep, its own threads, files or network calls. The SDK has deterministic versions, Workflow.randomUUID(), Workflow.currentTimeMillis() and Workflow.sleep(...), whose values come from the history on replay. Everything else belongs in activities, and Temporal's static checker, Workflow Check, catches many slips.

The harder case is your own deploy. Version 1 of the order workflow is charge, reserve, sleep, ship, and 40,000 orders are asleep in their 24-hour wait. Version 2 adds a fraud check before the charge. When a version-1 order wakes up on a version-2 worker, the worker replays it: the new code's first command is schedule CheckFraud, but the history says the first activity was Charge. The SDK stops with a NonDeterministicException. Temporal counts it as a failed workflow task and retries it, so the order stays open and stuck until you deploy code that matches its history.

There are two ways out. Patching keeps one path per history:

val version = Workflow.getVersion("fraud-check", Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION, 1)
if (version >= 1 && !activities.checkFraud(orderId, amountCents)) return "REJECTED"

The first time a run reaches getVersion for real, the SDK records a marker in the history with the newest version, 1. A version-1 history has no marker, so on replay getVersion returns DEFAULT_VERSION (-1) and the old path runs. When no older runs are left, delete the old branch but keep getVersion("fraud-check", 1, 1) for a while before removing it. The other way out is to never replay old histories on new code. Temporal's Worker Versioning, generally available in 2026, can pin each run to the deployment version it started on. Restate makes every deployment immutable, and in-flight invocations finish on the one they started on. Either way, replay saved production histories against new code in CI with WorkflowReplayer before you deploy.

A compiler can break determinism too. Kotlin 2.4 compiles a method reference such as activities::charge differently from Kotlin 2.2. Temporal's Java SDK up to 1.40 doesn't recognize the new form when you pass it to Async.function or Async.procedure, so it runs the call on a new workflow thread. That can change the order of commands, and workflows started under Kotlin 2.2 then fail with NonDeterministicException when they replay on code built with 2.4, with no source change at all. The fix reached the SDK's main branch in October 2026, after 1.40.0. The labs build with Kotlin 2.4.21 on SDK 1.40, so their workflow code calls activities directly and never passes method references to Async or Saga.

try.title: Replay a version-1 history against two version-2s
steps: Open ReplayDemo.kt and the three workflow classes in DemoOrders.kt: OrderV1, OrderV2Naive (fraud check added in front of the charge) and OrderV2 (the same change behind getVersion).
Predict which replay fails, and at which event.

code.title: ReplayDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.enc.l05.demo import io.temporal.testing.WorkflowReplayer /** * Records the history of an order that ran on version 1, then replays it against two versions of the new code, * the way a CI job replays histories saved from production before a deploy. */ fun main() { quiet() val history = newEnv().use { env -> val worker = startWorker(env.workflowClient, "worker-1", OrderV1::class.java, StepsImpl(FakeBank(true))) startOrder(env.workflowClient, "order-9").getResult(String::class.java) worker.kill() env.workflowClient.fetchHistory("order-9") } println("a version-1 history with ${history.events.size} events") for (code in listOf(OrderV2Naive::class.java, OrderV2::class.java)) { try { WorkflowReplayer.replayWorkflowExecution(history, code) println("${code.simpleName}: replays cleanly") } catch (e: Exception) { // the replayer wraps the error; dig out the NonDeterministicException's own message val text = generateSequence<Throwable>(e) { it.cause }.joinToString(" ") { it.message ?: "" } println("${code.simpleName}: " + text.substringAfter("error=").substringBefore(" {WorkflowTaskStartedEventId").replace("\n", "")) } } }

try.expect:
a version-1 history with 28 events
OrderV2Naive: io.temporal.worker.NonDeterministicException: [TMPRL1100] Failure handling event 5 of type 'EVENT_TYPE_ACTIVITY_TASK_SCHEDULED' during replay. [TMPRL1100] Command COMMAND_TYPE_SCHEDULE_ACTIVITY_TASK doesn't match event EVENT_TYPE_ACTIVITY_TASK_SCHEDULED with EventId=5 on check activityType with an expected value 'name: "CheckFraud"' and an actual value 'name: "Charge"'.
OrderV2: replays cleanly

Event 5 is the first scheduled activity. The naive version wanted to schedule CheckFraud there; the history says Charge. The patched version asks getVersion, finds no marker, takes the old path and matches every event. WorkflowReplayer is what a CI job runs over histories saved from production (fetched with WorkflowClient.fetchHistory) before a deploy.

refs.title: Temporal: Versioning in the Java SDK
Jack Kleeman: Solving durable execution's immutability problem (Restate, 2024)

analogy: A durable workflow is a recipe cook who writes every finished step in a kitchen logbook: "8:02 charged the card, ch_1. 8:03 reserved the item." If the cook collapses, the next cook doesn't start over or guess. They read the recipe from the top with the logbook open, skip every step the log says is done, use the results written there, and pick up at the first step with no entry. The analogy breaks in two places. A cook can glance at the stove and see that the water is already boiling; the engine sees only the log, so a step done but not yet logged gets done again, which is why each step carries a key. And a new cook will follow whatever recipe is in their hand: hand them an edited recipe and the log stops making sense.
world: Your payment flows already run on Temporal, so look for three things in the workflow code. Every activity that calls an issuer, a ledger or Kafka should take a key built from the workflow ID and step name, and the receiving system must honour it, since Temporal will retry that activity. Every change to a workflow class that has runs in flight needs Workflow.getVersion (or pinned deployments with Worker Versioning), and a CI job that replays a few hundred real histories with WorkflowReplayer catches the ones you miss. And after the upgrade to Kotlin 2.4, search the workflow code for Async.function( and Async.procedure( with a :: in the arguments: until a release after 1.40 includes the fix, replace each method reference with a direct call or a lambda, and replay histories started under Kotlin 2.2 before you ship.
mistake: Believing that durable execution makes the charge happen exactly once. Teams move a payment flow into Temporal, read "exactly once" in a talk or a vendor page, and drop the idempotency key from the call to the issuer because the engine now handles failures. Then a worker is OOM-killed after the issuer approved a charge and before the activity reported back, Temporal retries the activity, and the customer is charged twice. The engine kept its promise: it records the workflow's progress once. The fix is to treat every activity as at-least-once: pass the issuer a key built from the workflow ID and the step ("$workflowId/charge"), make the issuer or your own ledger deduplicate on it, and set a start-to-close timeout so a dead attempt is noticed in seconds.

compare.title: The same order, hand-built and as a Temporal workflow

a.label: Status column and sweeper
a.title: runs every minute
a.html: // every new process gets its own copy of this machinery val stuck = jdbc.query(""" SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE status <> 'SHIPPED' AND updated_at < now() - interval '5 minutes' FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100""") for (o in stuck) when (o.status) { "NEW" -> { bank.charge("${o.id}/charge", o); setStatus(o, "CHARGED") } "CHARGED" -> try { warehouse.reserve("${o.id}/reserve", o); setStatus(o, "RESERVED") } catch (e: OutOfStock) { setStatus(o, "REFUNDING") } "REFUNDING" -> { bank.refund("${o.id}/refund", o); setStatus(o, "REFUNDED") } "RESERVED" -> if (pickupDue(o)) { courier.ship("${o.id}/ship", o); setStatus(o, "SHIPPED") } }

b.label: Temporal workflow
b.title: replayed after any crash
b.html: override fun process(orderId: String, amountCents: Long, sku: String): String { val id = Workflow.getInfo().workflowId val chargeId = activities.charge("$id/charge", orderId, amountCents) val reservationId = try { activities.reserve("$id/reserve", orderId, sku) } catch (e: ActivityFailure) { activities.refund("$id/refund", chargeId) return "REFUNDED" } Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofHours(24)) // a durable timer, not a polling query activities.ship("$id/ship", orderId, reservationId) return "SHIPPED" }

compare.note: Both versions record progress durably and both need keys on every external call. The difference is where the process lives. On the left it is spread over a status column, a polling query, a lock (SKIP LOCKED, covered in the Transactions track) and a branch per status; the wait for pickup is a condition checked every minute, and a new step means new statuses. On the right the process is ordinary code read top to bottom, and the engine supplies the history, retries, timers and the move to another worker after a crash. The price on the right is determinism: that function must replay identically, so changing it needs getVersion or pinned deployments.

worked.title: Start one workflow per Kafka event, even when the event arrives twice

steps.say: A consumer starts an order workflow for each "order placed" event. Kafka can deliver an event twice, for example after a consumer crash before its offset commit (the Messaging track covers when). The workflow ID is your dedupe key, so build it from the order ID, never from a random UUID.
steps.code: val options = WorkflowOptions.newBuilder() .setWorkflowId("order-$orderId") // the business key .setTaskQueue("orders") .setWorkflowIdReusePolicy(WorkflowIdReusePolicy.WORKFLOW_ID_REUSE_POLICY_REJECT_DUPLICATE) .build()

steps.say: Start the run. While a run with that ID is open, a second start throws WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStarted: that is the duplicate delivery, so acknowledge the event and move on.
steps.code: fun startOrderOnce(client: WorkflowClient, orderId: String, amountCents: Long): Boolean = try { client.newUntypedWorkflowStub("OrderWorkflow", options).start(orderId, amountCents) true } catch (e: WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStarted) { false // already started by an earlier delivery }

steps.say: Mind the reuse policy. By default (ALLOW_DUPLICATE), once the first run has closed, the same ID may start a new run, so an event redelivered after the order finished would start the order again. REJECT_DUPLICATE keeps the ID taken for as long as the closed run's history is retained. StartOnceDemo.kt runs both deliveries and a late third one; with the default policy, the third line prints true.
steps.code:
$ ./gradlew :flow:demo -Pmain=sfz.enc.l05.demo.StartOnceDemoKt --console=plain -q
first delivery started a run:  true
second delivery started a run: false
after the run closed, a third:  false
cards charged: 1

lab.title: An order workflow that survives a dead worker and a deploy
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 10 fail within seconds, because the stub's TODO fails every workflow. They use temporal-testing's in-memory server inside the JVM: no Docker, no Temporal CLI, and the 24-hour wait is skipped.
Read OrderApi.kt (the interfaces), OrderActivitiesImpl.kt (finished activities that count their runs and can fail right after their side effect) and World.kt (the fake bank, warehouse and courier).
In OrderWorkflowImpl.kt, write process as version 1 had it: charge, reserve, Workflow.sleep(PICKUP_WAIT), ship, passing each activity a key built from Workflow.getInfo().workflowId and the step name.
Add the compensations: catch ActivityFailure around reserve (refund, return "REFUNDED") and around ship (release, refund, return "CANCELLED").

Add the fraud check at the top, behind Workflow.getVersion(FRAUD_CHECK_CHANGE, Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION, 1). Run all 10 tests. CrashAndUpgradeTest stops a worker in the middle of an order, and wakes a run started on OrderWorkflowV1 (in the test folder) on your code.

Break it on purpose: replace the getVersion call with val version = 1 and run ./gradlew :flow:test --tests 'sfz.enc.l05.CrashAndUpgradeTest'. Three tests fail: two with a NonDeterministicException at event 5, and one because your history no longer has a version marker. Put the call back.
hints: An activity that fails for good reaches workflow code as io.temporal.failure.ActivityFailure. Catch that, not ApplicationFailure, which is its cause.
Keys like "$id/charge" with val id = Workflow.getInfo().workflowId are the same on every retry and replay. java.util.UUID.randomUUID() in workflow code would differ on replay.

If the version-1 tests fail with a NonDeterministicException, either the fraud check runs before getVersion has answered, or your old path doesn't issue the same commands as OrderWorkflowV1, in the same order.

The harness makes a TODO or a non-determinism error fail the workflow at once (setFailWorkflowExceptionTypes in OrderHarness.kt). In production both only fail the workflow task, which Temporal retries until you deploy a fix.

drill.title: Write a patch from memory
drill.prompt: The order workflow with the fraud check is in production. The next version must send a receipt (an activity sendReceipt(key, orderId)) right after ship, without breaking runs that are asleep before ship or replaying past it. Write the lines from ship to return. Then compare. Which versions did you pass to getVersion, and where does the key come from?

answer.html: val id = Workflow.getInfo().workflowId activities.ship("$id/ship", orderId, reservationId) // histories recorded past this point without a marker replay as DEFAULT_VERSION and skip the receipt val receipt = Workflow.getVersion("send-receipt", Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION, 1) if (receipt >= 1) { activities.sendReceipt("$id/receipt", orderId) } return "SHIPPED"

recap: A process that calls several systems can die between any two calls, and no local transaction can include a card network. Running it again from the top charges twice.
A status column plus a sweeper works, with keys, but every process rebuilds the locks, retries, timers and keys, and spreads its logic over a column and a cron job.

A saga pairs each step with a compensation and, when a step fails for good, runs the compensations of finished steps newest first. It has no isolation, and compensations must be retryable and idempotent.

Durable execution records each step's result in a durable log (Temporal's event history, Restate's journal, DBOS's Postgres checkpoints). After a crash, a worker replays the code and skips every recorded step.
"Exactly once" means the workflow's progress is recorded once. Activities run at least once, so pass every external call a key built from the workflow ID and step.
Workflow code must replay identically. Change it with Workflow.getVersion or pinned deployments, test with WorkflowReplayer, and with Kotlin 2.4 on SDK 1.40 keep method references away from Async.

explain.prompt: Your team lead says: "Once the payment flow is on Temporal we can drop the idempotency keys. Temporal gives us exactly-once." Explain what Temporal guarantees and what it doesn't.
explain.answer: Temporal guarantees that the workflow's progress is durable and applied once. Every activity's result is recorded in the event history, and after a crash any worker replays the workflow code against that history, skipping steps that are already recorded, so the flow never forgets where it was and never re-decides a step it has finished. It does not guarantee that an activity's side effect happens once. A worker can charge the card and die before reporting success; the server then sees an unfinished attempt and retries it, and the card network sees a second request. Activities are at-least-once by design. So we keep the keys: build one per step from the workflow ID ("$workflowId/charge"), which is stable across retries and replays, and make the issuer or our ledger deduplicate on it. Exactly-once for the business is at-least-once execution plus deduplication.

deeper.html:
A workflow history can't grow forever. Temporal limits one run to 51,200 events or 50 MB and starts warning at 10,240 events or 10 MB. A workflow that loops, such as a subscription that charges every month for years, calls continue-as-new: it closes the current run and starts a fresh one with the same workflow ID, carrying its state over as input, so each history stays short.

Workflows can also take input while they run. In Temporal, a signal is an asynchronous message into a running workflow ("the courier collected the parcel"), a query reads its state without touching the history, and an update is a synchronous, validated write that is recorded once accepted. A human approval step is a workflow waiting for a signal, possibly for days, at no cost.

The Java SDK has a Saga helper class that collects compensations and runs them in reverse. Its addCompensation takes a function, and from Kotlin that tempts you to write saga.addCompensation(activities::refund, key, chargeId). Given the Kotlin 2.4 issue, pass a lambda instead, saga.addCompensation { activities.refund(key, chargeId) }, which behaves the same under every compiler version.

The idea is older than any of these engines. Microsoft's Durable Functions and Uber's Cadence, built by the engineers who went on to found Temporal, use the same history-and-replay model. For the book's framing of workflows, durable execution and its determinism caveats, see Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 5; the book returns to determinism in chapter 9, on the trouble with distributed systems.
